Task 1

Task 1 — Overall Crime Statistics

Volume, mix and geography of reported incidents, plus a live-feed snapshot of the most recent activity.

Incident volume by crime type across all cities.
Total reported incidents by city.
How incidents split across severity bands.
City locations sized by incident volume and coloured by the share of high-severity incidents.

Key findings

  • 1,000 incidents span 8 cities and 8 crime types over 2023-06-11 to 2025-06-10.
  • The most common incident is Vandalism (135 cases), followed by Theft and Homicide.
  • 251 incidents (25%) are high-severity; the volume leader is Austin (137 incidents).
  • Live-feed snapshot: 243 incidents logged in 2025; most recent = Theft in Little Rock on 2025-06-10 at 04:16.
Task 2

Task 2 — Time-Period Analysis

How incidents distribute across day of week, hour, and named time blocks — the timing signal behind preventive deployment.

Weekday vs. weekend incident volume.
Hourly reporting curve across the full period.
Morning 05–12, Afternoon 12–17, Evening 17–21, Night 21–05.
Density of incidents by weekday and hour.

Key findings

  • Busiest day is Tuesday (156 incidents); weekend share is 26% of all incidents.
  • Reporting peaks around 00:00 (53 incidents in that hour).
  • Night is the dominant time block at 32.8% of incidents; the split is Morning 30%, Afternoon 21%, Evening 16%, Night 33%.
Task 3

Task 3 — Trend Analysis

Change in reporting over time: monthly trajectory, same-month year-over-year comparison, and how the crime-type mix evolves.

Reported incidents per calendar month.
Month-by-month incident counts overlaid by year (partial first/last years reflect the data window).
Composition of incidents by crime type within each year.

Key findings

  • Yearly incident counts — 2023: 272, 2024: 485, 2025: 243. Note the first and last calendar years are partial given the 2023-06-11–2025-06-10 window.
  • Monthly volume averages 40 incidents (min 15, max 52), with no runaway seasonal spike — consistent with an evenly sampled dataset.
  • Crime-type mix stays broadly stable across years, so shifts are in volume/timing rather than the type of crime being committed.
Task 4

Task 4 — Comparative Analysis

Arrest outcomes compared across crime type and city, plus the severity composition of each category (adapted from the requested domestic breakdown, which the dataset cannot support).

Overall share of incidents resulting in an arrest.
Percentage of incidents per crime type ending in arrest.
Per-category severity mix — the closest available proxy for the 'domestic share' breakdown, since the dataset carries no Domestic flag.
How arrest outcomes vary across cities.

Key findings

  • 689 incidents (69%) resulted in an arrest vs. 311 with no arrest.
  • Arrest rate is highest for Homicide (100%) and lowest for Drug Offense (59%).
  • High-severity share peaks for Robbery (100% high). The dataset has no Domestic field, so this severity breakdown stands in for the requested domestic-category analysis.
  • City arrest rates range from 66% (Houston) to 74% (San Antonio).
Task 5

Task 5 — Cluster Analysis

Unsupervised segmentation: K-means groups individual incidents by when/where/how-severe they are, and hierarchical clustering groups cities by their crime-type signature.

Choosing the number of incident clusters. Silhouette is maximised at k=2.
Incidents projected to two principal components and coloured by cluster; black X = cluster centroids.
Each cluster's feature profile relative to the overall mean (red = above average, blue = below).
Cities grouped by the similarity of their crime-type mix.

Key findings

  • K-means on 5 circumstance features (hour, day, severity, lat, long) favours k=2 (silhouette 0.22); the two principal components capture 51% of variance, driven largely by geography (lat/long) and time-of-day.
  • The largest segment is Cluster 1 (634 incidents, top crime Theft in Austin, clearance/arrest rate 69%).
  • Arrest outcome was held out of the clustering and profiled afterwards: clearance is essentially uniform (~69%) across the geographic segments, i.e. clearance is not location-driven in this data — a useful negative result for resource planning.
  • Because location dominates the five features, the K-means segments are effectively regional; the silhouette also rises again at higher k (city-level granularity), so k is a resolution choice between broad regions and individual cities rather than a single 'true' number.
  • Hierarchical clustering of cities on their crime-type mix yields 3 city groups, useful for peer benchmarking and shared prevention strategy.
